content: Acute ear infections are one of the most common reasons parents bring their children to the doctor. The most frequent type of ear infection is called otitis media, which refers to inflammation and infection of the middle ear, located just behind the eardrum. An acute ear infection is typically short-lived but can be quite painful. Symptoms of Acute Ear Infections In infants, the primary signs often include irritability and inconsolable crying. Many infants and children with acute ear infections may also experience fever or difficulty sleeping. Tugging on the ear is not always a reliable indicator of an ear infection. In older children and adults, symptoms may include: Ear pain or earache A sensation of fullness in the ear General feelings of illness Vomiting Diarrhea Hearing loss in the affected ear The infection may develop shortly after a cold. Sudden drainage of yellow or green fluid from the ear could indicate a ruptured eardrum. All acute ear infections involve fluid accumulation behind the eardrum. Devices like electronic ear monitors (e.g., EarCheck) can detect this fluid at home, but a doctor’s confirmation is still necessary. Causes of Acute Ear Infections The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the throat and is responsible for draining fluid from the middle ear. If this tube becomes blocked, fluid can accumulate, leading to infection. Infants and children are more prone to ear infections because their Eustachian tubes are more easily clogged. Adults can also develop ear infections, though they are less common. Factors that can cause the Eustachian tubes to swell or become blocked include: Allergies Colds and sinus infections Excess mucus and saliva during teething Infected or enlarged adenoids Exposure to tobacco smoke or other irritants Drinking from a sippy cup or bottle while lying on the back can also increase the risk of ear infections in children. However, getting water in the ears does not cause acute ear infections unless the eardrum has a pre-existing hole. Acute ear infections are more common in winter. While ear infections are not contagious, colds that lead to them can spread among children. Risk Factors Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing acute ear infections, including: Attending daycare, especially with more than six children Changes in altitude or climate Living in a cold climate Exposure to smoke Genetic predisposition to infections Not being breastfed Pacifier use Recent ear infections or illnesses Diagnosis A healthcare provider will examine the ears using an otoscope, which may reveal: Areas of dullness or redness Air bubbles or fluid behind the eardrum Bloody fluid or pus in the middle ear A perforation (hole) in the eardrum A hearing test may be recommended for individuals with a history of ear infections. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your child’s doctor if: Pain, fever, or irritability does not improve within 24 to 48 hours The child appears sicker than expected for an ear infection The child has a high fever or severe pain Severe pain suddenly stops, which may indicate a ruptured eardrum Symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop, such as severe headache, dizziness, swelling around the ear, or facial muscle twitching For children under six months, notify the doctor immediately if the child has a fever, even without other symptoms. Treatment Options Some ear infections resolve on their own without antibiotics. Managing pain and allowing the body time to heal is often sufficient. Recommended measures include: Applying a warm cloth or warm water bottle to the affected ear Using over-the-counter pain relief ear drops or prescription ear drops for pain relief Taking over-the-counter medications like ibuprofen or acetaminophen for pain or fever (do not give aspirin to children) Children under six months with fever or symptoms should see a doctor. Older children may be monitored at home if they do not have a fever above 102°F, severe pain, or other medical issues. If symptoms worsen or do not improve, consult a healthcare provider to determine if antibiotics are necessary. Antibiotics Ear infections can be caused by viruses or bacteria. Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections. Many healthcare providers no longer prescribe antibiotics for every ear infection. However, antibiotics are typically given to children under six months with ear infections. Antibiotics are more likely to be prescribed if: The child is under two years old The child has a fever The child appears very ill Symptoms do not improve within 24 to 48 hours It is essential to complete the full course of antibiotics as prescribed, even if symptoms improve. If antibiotics do not seem effective within 48 to 72 hours, contact your doctor. A different antibiotic may be needed. Amoxicillin is often the first choice, but other options include azithromycin, clarithromycin, cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime, amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin), clindamycin, or ceftriaxone. Side effects of antibiotics may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Rarely, serious allergic reactions can occur. For children with recurrent infections, a smaller daily dose of antibiotics may be prescribed to prevent new infections. Surgery If infections persist despite treatment or if a child experiences frequent infections over a short period, ear tubes may be recommended. This procedure involves inserting a tiny tube into the eardrum to allow air to enter and fluid to drain more easily. Tympanostomy tube insertion is performed under general anesthesia, and the tubes usually fall out on their own. If they do not, they can be removed in the doctor’s office. If the adenoids are enlarged, surgical removal may be considered, especially if ear infections persist. Removing tonsils does not appear to help with ear infections. Prevention To reduce the risk of ear infections: Wash hands and toys frequently. Choose a daycare with six or fewer children to reduce exposure to colds and infections. Avoid pacifiers. Breastfeed, as it lowers the risk of ear infections. If bottle-feeding, hold the infant in an upright position. Avoid exposing children to secondhand smoke. Ensure immunizations are up-to-date, including the pneumococcal vaccine, which prevents infections from bacteria commonly causing ear infections. Avoid overusing antibiotics to prevent antibiotic resistance. Outlook Ear infections can be treated but may recur. They can be painful, and it is crucial to complete any prescribed antibiotics. Possible Complications Most ear infections are minor and resolve without complications. Temporary hearing loss during and after an infection is common due to lingering fluid in the ear. Other potential complications include: Ruptured or perforated eardrum Chronic or recurrent ear infections Enlarged adenoids or tonsils Formation of an abscess or cyst (cholesteatoma) from chronic infections Speech or language delays in children with lasting hearing loss from recurrent infections
